title: Vale Strip Balance
public_context: The Vale Institute and its bead-strip registry are fictional. Clerks compare finite, nonempty rows of integer labels and sometimes discuss a row after every label is increased by the same amount or after the row is read backward. The registry uses a numerical balance for filing related strips. Its scoring convention is withheld from this public description; the dossier gives the complete construction and examples.
source_text:
At the fictional Vale Institute, a strip is a finite, nonempty ordered row of integer labels. Its balance is computed by numbering positions from the left, beginning with one. Add the labels in odd-numbered positions to obtain O, and add those in even-numbered positions to obtain E. The registered balance is |O − E|, the absolute difference; it is never the signed difference. Position parity depends on a label's place in the row, not on whether the label itself is odd or even.

In daily work, the balance is a quick shelf index: strips with similar balances are filed nearby so clerks can find candidates before checking a full row. It is not a unique identifier; different strips can share one balance, and the labels remain the definitive record.

For the strip [4, 1, 6], O = 4 + 6 = 10 and E = 1, so the balance is 9. For [4, 1, 6, 3], O = 4 + 6 = 10 and E = 1 + 3 = 4, giving 6. Reading that four-label strip backward gives [3, 6, 1, 4]: O = 3 + 1 = 4 and E = 6 + 4 = 10, so its balance is also 6. Reversal preserves the result because it either keeps the two position groups in place or exchanges them, and the absolute difference is unchanged.

Uniform changes have a length-dependent consequence. Adding 2 to every entry of the three-label strip gives [6, 3, 8], with O = 14 and E = 3; the balance rises from 9 to 11. For an even-length strip, adding the same amount contributes equally to O and E, so the balance is unchanged: [4, 1, 6, 3] becomes [6, 3, 8, 5], with O = 14 and E = 8, still giving 6. These identities follow from the construction and apply to any integer labels. The institute records no balance for an empty strip.

core_facts: Positions are numbered from the left starting at one; odd and even positions define the two sums.
The balance is the absolute difference between the odd-position and even-position sums.
Reversing a strip leaves its balance unchanged.
Adding a constant to every entry leaves an even-length balance unchanged; for odd length, the signed alternating sum changes by that constant before taking absolute value.
explicit_negations: The score is not the signed difference; it is the absolute difference.
Position parity is not determined by whether a label is odd or even.
source_boundaries: The construction is defined here for finite, nonempty rows of integer labels.
No weighted, circular, or empty-row extension is defined.
consistency_checks: [4,1,6] gives odd-position sum 10, even-position sum 1, and balance 9.
[4,1,6,3] and its reversal [3,6,1,4] both give balance 6.
Adding 2 to all entries changes the three-item example's balance to 11 and keeps the four-item example's balance at 6.
